name: ʿAin Mallaha (Eynan)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the village is known from excavations and radiocarbon dates on bones and charcoal.
summary: A Natufian village of round stone-based huts beside the old Lake Hula in northern Israel. Its people still hunted and gathered wild food, yet they lived here all year round, one of the earliest examples of settled life before farming. They buried their dead under and around the houses. One grave held an elderly person with a hand resting on a puppy, among the oldest evidence for a close bond between people and dogs.

name: Raqefet Cave
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the burials are dated by radiocarbon, and the claim that people brewed beer here is still debated.
summary: A cave on Mount Carmel in Israel used by Natufian foragers as a cemetery. Impressions of stems, leaves and flowers in the mud lining of several graves suggest the dead were laid on beds of flowering plants, the oldest known example of this custom. Stone mortars cut into the cave floor held traces of cereals; one team argued in 2018 that they were used to make a kind of beer, but other scholars think they were for grinding flour.

image.caption: Entrance to Raqefet Cave on Mount Carmel

name: Tell Abu Hureyra
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from a rescue dig in 1972–73 and radiocarbon dates on seeds and bones.
summary: A mound on the Euphrates in Syria that records the switch from foraging to farming in one place. The first village belonged to hunter-gatherers; plant remains suggest they began cultivating rye around 13,000 years ago, possibly the earliest cereal farming known. A later, much larger farming village of mudbrick houses followed. The site was excavated in a hurry before the Tabqa Dam flooded it, and it now lies under Lake Assad.

name: Tassili n'Ajjer rock art
dateLabel: c. 10,000 BCE (debated) to the early centuries CE
evidenceNote: The paintings are real, but they are very hard to date and scholars disagree by thousands of years about how old the earliest styles are.
summary: A sandstone plateau in the Algerian Sahara holding thousands of rock paintings and engravings made over many millennia, when the Sahara was greener. The styles are grouped in a sequence: early wild animals, the 'Round Head' figures, scenes of cattle herders, and later pictures of horses, chariots and camels. Together they show how life changed as the Sahara dried out. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and national park.

name: Jericho (Tell es-Sultan)
dateLabel: c. 10,000 BCE – Persian period; tower and wall c. 8000 BCE
evidenceNote: The Neolithic town is dated by excavation and radiocarbon; excavators found no walled city at the time the Bible's story of Joshua is usually placed.
summary: One of the oldest continuously settled places on Earth, beside a strong spring near the Dead Sea. By about 8000 BCE the farming town was enclosed by a stone wall over 3.6 m high, with an 8.5 m stone tower inside, among the oldest monumental buildings known. Kathleen Kenyon excavated the tower in the 1950s. Later Bronze Age Jericho was destroyed in the 16th century BCE; the Bible's tale of its walls falling is not supported by the excavations.

image.caption: The Neolithic stone tower at Tell es-Sultan (Jericho)

name: Karahan Tepe
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the site has been dug only since 2019 and its dates come from a small but growing set of radiocarbon samples.
summary: A Stone Age site in Şanlıurfa province, Turkey, about 46 km east of Göbekli Tepe and closely related to it. Builders cut rooms into the bedrock and set up T-shaped pillars; one chamber holds a carved human head emerging from the wall above a row of stone pillars. It belongs to the 'Taş Tepeler' (Stone Hills), a group of about a dozen similar sites now being excavated, which show that Göbekli Tepe was not unique.

image.caption: Carved stone pillars in a rock-cut room at Karahan Tepe

name: Göbekli Tepe
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything we know comes from excavations since 1995 and radiocarbon dates.
summary: A hilltop in southeastern Turkey where people built round enclosures of huge T-shaped limestone pillars, the tallest about 5 m high, about 11,500 years ago, among the oldest known megaliths. Many pillars are carved with foxes, boars, snakes and vultures, and some have arms and belts, suggesting stylised humans. First seen as a temple used by roaming hunters, it is now known to have had houses, cisterns and heavy cereal processing. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: Excavated enclosures with T-shaped stone pillars at Göbekli Tepe

name: Çayönü
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is dated by excavations from 1964 to 1991 and radiocarbon.
summary: An early farming village near Diyarbakır in southeastern Turkey, at the foot of the Taurus Mountains near a tributary of the Tigris. Over two thousand years its people moved from round huts to rectangular houses on stone 'grill' foundations, built special public buildings, and worked copper and malachite. Its people grew emmer and einkorn wheat, and it is a key site for the early domestication of pigs and cattle.

image.caption: The mound of Çayönü below the Taurus foothills

name: Nabta Playa
dateLabel: c. 7500–3500 BCE; stone circle 5th millennium BCE
evidenceNote: The camps, cattle burials and stones are real and dated by radiocarbon, but whether the stone circle was really an astronomical calendar is debated.
summary: A seasonal lake basin in the Egyptian desert about 100 km west of Abu Simbel, visited by herders when the Sahara was wetter. They dug wells, built huts in rows, made early pottery and buried cattle under stone mounds. A small ring of upright stones, the 'calendar circle', and lines of larger stones have been claimed as alignments to the summer solstice and to certain stars; some proposed alignments have been rejected by other researchers.

image.caption: Reconstruction of the Nabta Playa stone circle at the Nubia Museum, Aswan

name: ʿAin Ghazal
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the village and its statues are dated by excavation and radiocarbon.
summary: A large Neolithic farming town on the edge of modern Amman, Jordan, which around 7000 BCE covered 10–15 hectares and housed perhaps 3,000 people. It is famous for 15 statues and 15 busts of lime plaster built over reed frames, with staring eyes outlined in bitumen, found buried in two pits in 1983 and 1985. Made between about 7200 and 6250 BCE, they are among the oldest large human figures ever found. Many are now in the Jordan Museum.

image.caption: One of the plaster statues from ʿAin Ghazal

name: Çatalhöyük
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavations since 1958 and radiocarbon dates.
summary: A very large Neolithic town on the Konya Plain in central Turkey, home to several thousand people. Houses were packed so tightly that there were no streets: people walked over the roofs and climbed in through holes. Rooms were decorated with wall paintings, plaster bull heads and horns, and the dead were buried beneath the floors. Houses look much alike, which suggests a fairly equal society. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.

image.caption: Excavated mudbrick houses under the protective roof at Çatalhöyük

name: Jarmo
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the village is dated by excavations in the 1940s–50s and radiocarbon.
summary: A small farming village in the Zagros foothills of Iraqi Kurdistan, among oak and pistachio woods. Robert Braidwood of the University of Chicago's Oriental Institute excavated it to find where farming began. Its people grew early wheat and barley and kept goats and sheep, living in mud-walled houses. Jarmo showed that the hilly flanks of the Fertile Crescent, not only river valleys, were where agriculture took root.

name: Ugarit (Ras Shamra)
dateLabel: c. 7000–1185 BCE; golden age c. 1500–1200 BCE
evidenceNote: Thousands of clay tablets found in the city, in several languages, describe its kings, trade and religion.
summary: A port city on the Syrian coast north of Latakia, settled since the Neolithic. In its golden age, about 1500–1200 BCE, it ruled a small trading kingdom linked to Egypt, Cyprus, the Aegean and the Hittites. Its archives include tablets in a cuneiform alphabet of 30 letters, one of the oldest alphabets known, and myths of the god Baal. The city was destroyed around 1185 BCE during the Late Bronze Age collapse.

name: Tell Halaf
dateLabel: c. 6100–5400 BCE (Halaf village); later the Aramaean city of Guzana
evidenceNote: The Neolithic village had no writing and is dated by excavation; the later city of Guzana is named in Assyrian texts.
summary: A mound near Ras al-Ayn in northeastern Syria that gave its name to the Halaf culture, famous for finely painted pottery with geometric and animal designs. Max von Oppenheim dug here from 1911, mostly exposing the much later palace of the Aramaean city of Guzana with stone statues and reliefs. Many of those finds were smashed when a Berlin museum was bombed in 1943 and have since been pieced back together.

image.caption: Excavated remains of the northeast palace at Tell Halaf

name: Eridu
evidenceNote: The early temples are known from excavation; later Sumerian texts name Eridu and call it the first city.
summary: A mound in southern Iraq that Sumerian tradition remembered as the oldest city, where kingship first came down from heaven. Excavators found eighteen mudbrick temples built one on top of another, beginning with a tiny shrine of the Ubaid period and growing into a large platform temple, which shows how Mesopotamian temples developed over time. The city's god was Enki. The ruins of a ziggurat of Ur-Nammu still stand.

image.caption: Baked bricks of the ziggurat at Eridu

name: Uruk (Eanna and the White Temple)
dateLabel: c. 5000 BCE – c. 700 CE; Eanna and White Temple c. 3500–3100 BCE
evidenceNote: Uruk is where some of the earliest writing was found, and it is named in thousands of later texts.
summary: The great city of southern Iraq that gave its name to the Uruk period. Around 3100 BCE it may have held up to 50,000 people, probably the largest town in the world then. In the Eanna temple district of the goddess Inanna archaeologists found some of the oldest written tablets; the White Temple, whitewashed and set on a high terrace, stood in the Anu district. Later tradition made Gilgamesh a king of Uruk.

image.caption: The Anu ziggurat at Uruk, base of the White Temple

name: Areni-1 cave
evidenceNote: No writing existed; finds are dated by radiocarbon and kept well by the cave's dry, cool air.
summary: A cave beside the Arpa River in southern Armenia used by Copper Age people for storage, rituals and burials. Its dry air preserved remarkable things: a one-piece leather shoe about 5,500 years old, the oldest leather footwear known, and a winemaking installation of about 4100–4000 BCE, described as the oldest known winery. Burials and storage jars show the cave also had ritual uses.

image.caption: The Arpa River gorge with the Areni-1 cave

name: Susa
evidenceNote: Excavated since the 1850s and named in Elamite, Mesopotamian, Persian and Greek writings.
summary: One of the oldest cities in the world, in Khuzestan, southwestern Iran, between the Karkheh and Dez rivers. It was founded around 4200 BCE, became the capital of Elam, and later served as a capital of the Persian kings, who built a great palace here. The famous law code stele of Hammurabi was found at Susa in 1901, where Elamite raiders had carried it. The modern town of Shush stands on the site.

name: Hierakonpolis (Nekhen)
evidenceNote: The early town is dated by excavation and radiocarbon; writing appears only at the very end, on objects such as the Narmer Palette.
summary: The leading town of Upper Egypt before the pharaohs, about 100 km south of Luxor. Already by 3600 BCE it stretched over 3 km along the Nile, with breweries, potteries, a temple to the falcon god Horus and an elite cemetery. Its 'Painted Tomb' has the oldest known Egyptian tomb painting. The Narmer Palette, which shows a king of about 3100 BCE triumphing over enemies, was found here.

sources.title: Hierakonpolis Expedition: Firsts of the First City

name: Arslantepe
evidenceNote: The early palace had no writing and is dated by radiocarbon; the later city of Melid appears in Hittite and Assyrian texts.
summary: A mound near Malatya in eastern Turkey on a tributary of the Euphrates. Around 3400–3200 BCE it had a mudbrick temple-palace complex with clay sealings for controlling goods, an early example of a state-like administration in contact with Uruk Mesopotamia. In it archaeologists found some of the oldest known swords, made of arsenic bronze. Much later it was a Neo-Hittite city with lion sculptures. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.

name: Abydos
evidenceNote: The early royal tombs are known from excavation and early inscriptions; later texts and temples name it as Osiris's holy city.
summary: A sacred site in Upper Egypt whose desert cemetery, Umm el-Qaab, holds the tombs of Egypt's first kings, from before the First Dynasty to the Second. Later Egyptians believed the god Osiris was buried here, and pilgrims came for his festival for thousands of years. The temple of Seti I, built around 1290 BCE, contains the Abydos King List, which names most earlier pharaohs in order.

image.caption: Temple of Seti I at Abydos

name: Ur (ziggurat and Royal Cemetery)
dateLabel: c. 3800–500 BCE; Royal Cemetery c. 2600 BCE; ziggurat 21st century BCE
evidenceNote: Ur is named in many cuneiform texts, and its kings left inscriptions on the ziggurat's bricks.
summary: A major Sumerian city in southern Iraq, once near the Persian Gulf coast. Leonard Woolley's digs (1922–34) uncovered the Royal Cemetery of about 2600 BCE, where rulers such as Queen Puabi were buried with gold, lyres, the 'Standard of Ur' and dozens of attendants who died with them. The great ziggurat was built by King Ur-Nammu in the 21st century BCE and restored by Nabonidus about 1,500 years later.

image.caption: The Ziggurat of Ur, with its partly rebuilt facade

name: Maykop kurgan
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the tomb was dug in 1897 and is dated by comparing its objects and by radiocarbon dates from related graves.
summary: A burial mound about 10 m high in the town of Maykop in the North Caucasus of Russia, excavated by Nikolay Veselovsky in 1897. Under it lay a chieftain or 'priest-king' with rich grave goods, including gold and silver bull figurines, and the burials of two women. It gave its name to the Maykop culture, and its treasures are now in the Hermitage Museum. The mound itself no longer survives.

name: Troy (Hisarlik)
evidenceNote: The city's ruins are real, and most scholars accept Hisarlik as Homer's Troy, but there is no firm proof that the Trojan War of legend happened.
summary: A mound near the Dardanelles in northwest Turkey with nine main layers of cities built on top of each other over about 4,000 years. Heinrich Schliemann and Frank Calvert dug it from 1871 looking for Homer's Troy. In the Late Bronze Age the city was probably the Wilusa named in Hittite texts, and one layer was destroyed around 1180 BCE. Whether any of this matches the war in the Iliad remains unproven.

image.caption: Walls of Bronze Age Troy

name: Ebla (Tell Mardikh)
dateLabel: c. 3500 BCE – 7th century CE; archives c. 2400–2300 BCE
evidenceNote: Its own clay-tablet archive, written in cuneiform, names its kings and trade partners.
summary: A city southwest of Aleppo in Syria that became the strongest kingdom of the region in the 3rd millennium BCE. In its royal palace Paolo Matthiae's Italian team found an archive of thousands of clay tablets from about 2400–2300 BCE, written in a previously unknown language now called Eblaite. Its discovery proved that Syria had cities and states as old as those of Egypt and Mesopotamia.

image.caption: Excavated southern district of Ebla

name: Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn
evidenceNote: No local writing survives; the tombs and towers are dated by excavation, while Sumerian texts mention a copper land called Magan.
summary: A group of Bronze Age sites in inland Oman. Hundreds of stone 'beehive' tombs line the ridges, and round stone towers stood near a palm grove. They belong to the Hafit and Umm an-Nar periods, when this region exported copper and stone to Mesopotamia; the area is usually identified with the land of Magan in Sumerian texts. Together they form one of the most complete Bronze Age landscapes in Arabia, a UNESCO site since 1988.

image.caption: A beehive tomb at Al-Ayn, part of the Bat World Heritage group

sources.title: Wikipedia: Archaeological Sites of Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn

name: Nineveh
dateLabel: c. 3000–612 BCE (Assyrian capital from c. 700 BCE)
evidenceNote: Named in Assyrian royal inscriptions and the Bible; its palace libraries held tens of thousands of tablets.
summary: An ancient city on the east bank of the Tigris opposite Mosul in northern Iraq. Under Sennacherib it became the capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire and for a few decades probably the largest city in the world, with huge palaces, gates and canals. The library of Ashurbanipal, dug up here, held about 22,000 clay tablets. Nineveh was sacked in 612 BCE by Babylonians, Medes and others. Parts of the site were damaged during the war with ISIS.

image.caption: The reconstructed Mashki Gate of Nineveh, later destroyed by the Islamic State

name: Step Pyramid of Djoser, Saqqara
evidenceNote: Built for a king whose name is written in the complex, and dated by Egyptian king lists and radiocarbon.
summary: The first Egyptian pyramid, built in the 27th century BCE at Saqqara near Memphis for King Djoser of the Third Dynasty. Its six stacked steps grew out of several changes of plan, and it was once covered in white limestone. It is the earliest colossal building in Egypt made of cut stone, and the start of the pyramid age. Later Egyptians credited its design to the official Imhotep.

image.caption: The Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara

name: Pyramids of Giza
evidenceNote: The pyramids are dated by Egyptian king lists, workers' graffiti naming the kings, and radiocarbon.
summary: The burial complex of three kings of Egypt's Fourth Dynasty, Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure, at the edge of the desert west of Cairo. Khufu's Great Pyramid was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for almost 4,000 years and is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing. The site also includes the Great Sphinx, temples, cemeteries for officials, and the village of the workers who built them.

image.caption: The pyramids of Giza

name: Kerma
evidenceNote: The Kerma people left no writing of their own; we know them from excavation and from Egyptian records that call their land Kush.
summary: Capital of the first great kingdom of Nubia, beside the Nile in northern Sudan. Its centre was the Western Deffufa, a massive mudbrick temple that still towers over the ruins. In the great cemetery to the east, rulers were buried under round mounds with cattle skulls and, in later periods, sacrificed people. At its peak, about 1750–1500 BCE, Kerma was a rival of Egypt, until the armies of Thutmose I campaigned south and destroyed it.

image.caption: The Western Deffufa, the great mudbrick temple of Kerma

name: Babylon
dateLabel: c. 2300 BCE – c. 1000 CE; first mentioned c. 2200 BCE
evidenceNote: Babylon appears in thousands of cuneiform texts, in Greek histories and in the Bible.
summary: The great city on the Euphrates south of Baghdad, capital of Hammurabi's kingdom in the 18th century BCE and of Nebuchadnezzar II's empire in the 6th century BCE. Nebuchadnezzar rebuilt it with massive walls, the blue-glazed Ishtar Gate and the temple of Marduk with its ziggurat, Etemenanki. The Hanging Gardens may never have existed: no Babylonian text mentions them. Babylon became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.

image.caption: Modern replica of the Ishtar Gate at Babylon (the original bricks are in Berlin)

name: Dilmun Burial Mounds
evidenceNote: The mounds are dated by excavation; Mesopotamian texts describe Dilmun as a trading land in the Gulf.
summary: Thousands of burial mounds across the north of Bahrain, once one of the largest ancient cemeteries in the world; an estimated 350,000 graves may have existed. Most were built during the time of Dilmun, the Gulf trading civilisation that linked Mesopotamia with the Indus Valley; Bahrain's freshwater springs made it a natural stop for ships. The surviving mound fields became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.

image.caption: Burial mounds in Bahrain, photographed in 1918

name: Hattusa
dateLabel: c. 2000–1190 BCE (Hittite capital from c. 1650 BCE)
evidenceNote: Tens of thousands of clay tablets found in the city record Hittite laws, treaties and letters.
summary: The capital of the Hittite kings, inside a bend of the Kızılırmak River in central Turkey. Its walls, gates guarded by stone lions and sphinxes, temples and palaces covered a hilly site of about 1.8 km². Its archives of clay tablets, and a bronze tablet recording a treaty between King Tudhaliya IV and Kurunta of Tarhuntassa, reveal Hittite politics. The city was abandoned around 1190 BCE when the Hittite empire collapsed.

image.caption: The Lion Gate in the walls of Hattusa

name: Palmyra
dateLabel: early 2nd millennium BCE – 1932 CE; height 1st–3rd century CE
evidenceNote: Palmyra is named in texts from about 2000 BCE, and thousands of its own inscriptions survive.
summary: An oasis city in the Syrian desert that grew rich on caravan trade between the Roman Empire, Mesopotamia and beyond. Its merchants paid for the Great Colonnade, the Temple of Bel (dedicated in 32 CE) and tall tower tombs. In the 260s its rulers Odaenathus and then Queen Zenobia briefly controlled much of the Roman East, until Rome sacked the city in 273 CE. ISIS blew up the Temple of Bel and other monuments in 2015.

image.caption: Ruins of Palmyra with the Temple of Bel behind (photo before 2015)

name: Karnak Temple Complex
evidenceNote: Its walls are covered with hieroglyphic inscriptions naming the kings who built each part.
summary: The vast temple of the god Amun at Thebes (modern Luxor), the main religious centre of New Kingdom Egypt. Building began under Senusret I around 1970 BCE and continued for nearly 2,000 years, into Ptolemaic times. Its Great Hypostyle Hall has 134 giant columns. A processional avenue lined with sphinxes connected it to Luxor Temple. Karnak is part of the UNESCO site of Ancient Thebes.

image.caption: Hall of columns at Karnak, in a 19th-century photograph

name: Etemenanki, the ziggurat of Babylon
dateLabel: origins perhaps 18th century BCE; rebuilt 7th–6th century BCE; demolished 323 BCE
evidenceNote: The ziggurat is described in Babylonian inscriptions and a tablet giving its size; only its foundation outline survives.
summary: The great stepped temple tower of the god Marduk in Babylon, whose name means 'Temple of the Foundation of Heaven and Earth'. Damaged when Sennacherib sacked Babylon in 689 BCE, it was rebuilt by Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II. A later tablet claims it was 91 m high and wide, a figure modern scholars doubt. Alexander the Great had it pulled down in 323 BCE to rebuild it, but died first. Today only a water-filled square marks its base.

name: Tower of Babel (legend)
dateLabel: Legend; no date can be given
evidenceNote: Not proven: no archaeological evidence has been found for the tower of the Genesis story; many scholars think Babylon's real Etemenanki ziggurat may have inspired it, but that link is a hypothesis.
summary: In chapter 11 of the Book of Genesis, people who all speak one language build a city and a tower reaching to the sky in the land of Shinar (southern Mesopotamia), and God scatters them by confusing their speech. It is an origin story for the world's many languages, not a historical record. Because the Hebrew name Babel means Babylon, modern scholars most often link the tale to the city's huge ziggurat, Etemenanki. The marker is placed there only to show that link.

name: Luxor Temple
evidenceNote: Inscriptions on the temple name its builders, Amenhotep III, Tutankhamun, Ramesses II and Alexander.
summary: A large temple on the east bank of the Nile in Luxor (ancient Thebes), begun around 1400 BCE by Amenhotep III. It was dedicated to the renewal of kingship, and statues of Amun were carried here from Karnak each year in the Opet festival. Ramesses II added the front pylon, colossal statues and two obelisks; one now stands in Paris. In Roman times it became part of a legionary fort, and a mosque still stands on its walls.

image.caption: Entrance pylon and obelisk of Luxor Temple at night

name: Abu Simbel temples
evidenceNote: Inscriptions carved in the temples name Ramesses II and his queen Nefertari.
summary: Two temples cut into a sandstone cliff in Nubia, in the far south of Egypt, by Ramesses II in the 13th century BCE. Four colossal seated statues of the king guard the Great Temple, while the smaller temple honours Queen Nefertari; reliefs inside celebrate his battle of Kadesh. In the 1960s an international campaign cut both temples into blocks and moved them uphill, away from the rising waters of Lake Nasser.

image.caption: The Great and Small Temples at Abu Simbel

name: Chogha Zanbil
evidenceNote: Inscribed bricks name its gods, and Elamite records link it to King Untash-Napirisha.
summary: A religious city of the Elamite king Untash-Napirisha in Khuzestan, southwestern Iran, southeast of Susa. Its centre is one of the few ziggurats outside Mesopotamia and the best preserved anywhere; thousands of its bricks carry inscriptions. The city is usually thought to have been destroyed by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal around 645 BCE, though some researchers think it was abandoned much earlier. It was Iran's first UNESCO site, in 1979.

image.caption: The Elamite ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil

name: Carthage
dateLabel: founded c. 814 BCE (traditional date); destroyed 146 BCE; Roman city to 698 CE
evidenceNote: Greek and Roman writers describe the city; its founding date of 814 BCE comes from later tradition rather than from excavation.
summary: A city on the coast of Tunisia founded by Phoenician settlers from Tyre, traditionally in 814 BCE. It grew into the capital of a trading empire across the western Mediterranean and fought Rome in the three Punic Wars, including Hannibal's invasion of Italy. Rome destroyed it in 146 BCE; Julius Caesar founded a new city on the site, which became one of the largest in the Roman West until its destruction in 698 CE. Traces of its circular naval harbour survive. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Meroë
dateLabel: c. 800 BCE – 350 CE; royal pyramids c. 300 BCE – 350 CE
evidenceNote: Meroitic inscriptions can be read aloud but are still not fully understood; Egyptian, Greek and Roman texts also describe Meroë.
summary: The capital of the Kingdom of Kush beside the Nile north of Khartoum in Sudan, from about 590 BCE to the 4th century CE. More than 200 steep-sided Nubian pyramids stand in its cemeteries, built for kings and queens from about 300 BCE. The city was a centre of iron-working and trade between Africa and the Mediterranean, and its rulers included powerful queens called kandake. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: Pyramids of the Kushite royal cemetery at Meroë

name: Great Dam of Marib
evidenceNote: Sabaean and Himyarite inscriptions record its building and repairs; its final collapse is remembered in the Qur'an.
summary: An ancient earth-and-stone dam across Wadi Adhanah near Marib in Yemen, first built in the 8th century BCE and enlarged many times. By catching the sudden floods it watered about 100 km² of fields that fed the Sabaean kingdom, famous for its incense trade. Its stone sluices still stand. After repeated breaches it finally failed in the late 6th century CE. The Marib monuments became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.

image.caption: Ruins of the ancient Marib Dam sluice works

name: Behistun inscription
evidenceNote: It is itself a written source, carved for Darius the Great in three languages.
summary: A huge relief and inscription carved high on a cliff at Mount Behistun near Kermanshah in western Iran, on the orders of Darius the Great after he seized the Persian throne in 522 BCE. It tells his version of how he defeated rebels, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Like the Rosetta Stone for Egyptian, its three matching texts let scholars in the 19th century decipher cuneiform writing. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: Darius the Great's relief and inscription at Behistun

name: Persepolis
evidenceNote: Royal inscriptions on the buildings and thousands of administrative tablets document its construction.
summary: The ceremonial capital of the Persian (Achaemenid) Empire on the plain of Marvdasht in southern Iran, begun by Darius the Great around 518 BCE. On a great stone terrace stood audience halls with forests of columns. Staircase reliefs show delegations from across the empire bringing gifts to the king. Alexander the Great captured it in 330 BCE, and soon after the palaces burned. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: The Palace of Darius (Tachara) at Persepolis

name: Petra
dateLabel: c. 4th century BCE – 7th century CE; Treasury 1st century CE
evidenceNote: Nabataean inscriptions and Greek and Roman writers describe the city.
summary: The 'Rose City' of the Nabataeans, carved into red sandstone cliffs in southern Jordan. It grew rich as a hub of the incense trade and became the capital of the Nabataean kingdom. Its builders cut grand tomb facades such as the Treasury (Al-Khazneh) straight into the rock, and channels and cisterns stored scarce water. Rome annexed it in 106 CE; it declined after an earthquake in 363 CE. It is a UNESCO site.

image.caption: The Treasury (Al-Khazneh) at Petra lit by candles

name: Hegra (Mada'in Salih)
dateLabel: 1st century BCE – Roman period; tombs mainly 1st century CE
evidenceNote: Many tomb facades carry dated Nabataean inscriptions naming their owners.
summary: The second city of the Nabataean kingdom after Petra, near Al-'Ula in northwestern Saudi Arabia. More than 110 well-preserved tombs are carved into sandstone outcrops, many with inscriptions giving their owner and date. The settlement grew mainly in the 1st century CE under King Aretas IV and passed to Rome in 106 CE. Dry air and no later rebuilding have kept it in excellent condition. It was Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO site, in 2008.
